newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Tobacco ad bans fuel hunt for new marketing methods.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tobacco ad bans fuel hunt for new marketing methods.

text.p: Bans on tobacco advertising will force cigarette makers to seek marketing opportunities by exploiting loopholes.

After Friday's landmark U.S. settlement under which tobacco companies accepted restrictions on direct advertising, moves in Britain to ban tobacco advertising could serve as a model for other markets.
Since its election in May, Britain's first Labour government in 18 years has taken an increasingly hard-line on its proposed tobacco advertsing ban.
In addition to proposing a ban on all media advertising, the government now says it seeks to end sponsorship deals by tobacco companies and even merchandising-related promotions.

"If we are going to see a positive effect, then we have to cover all avenues of tobacco promotion -- magazine advertising and billboard advertising, but also all those related activities, all promotions," a spokesman for the Health Education Authority told Reuters.

Cigarette advertising has long been banned on television and radio, but the government insists a much wider ban is needed to combat what it calls the country's most preventable cause of death and disease.
"Smoking in its present form in this country kills about 121,000 people a year, that's 313 per day," the said.
TOBACCO INDUSTRY WILL FIND ALTERNATIVE METHODS

The tobacco industry is lobbying to convince the government to at least soften its stance, if not abandon the ban outright. The industry itself says some 15 million consumers spent about 12 billion pounds ($19.6 billion) on tobacco products in Britain in 1996.
"The tobacco industry obviously are very skilled at marketing. They'll find other ways of getting their message across," the Health Education Authority spokesman said.

"I would think if they are faced with a ban they will look for other means of advertising and promotion," John Carlisle, executive director for industry affairs for Britain's Tobacco Manufacturers' Association (TMA), told Reuters.
Marketing and promotional efforts by tobacco companies

that transcend traditional advertising avenues already include the sale of branded merchandise -- such as Philip Morris's Marlboro Classics clothes and RJR Nabisco Holdings' Camel footwear. Both feature the rugged, outdoor image of the American west used for years to promote both cigarettes.

Tobacco companies also sponsor promotions in British bars and clubs where free samples are distributed to smokers, and they underwrite magazines aimed at smokers that allow companies to collect valuable data-base marketing information.
The TMA's Carlisle declined to comment on what tack the tobacco makers might take if a stringent ban is introduced.

"We cannot forecast what companies will do if such a ban took place," he said. Any such information would have to come from the individual companies themselves, but he cautioned, "I doubt you'll get a lot out of them.
Advertising industry officials, however, clearly expect tobacco companies to rely increasingly on marketing directly to consumers if an ad ban is introduced.

"A lot of people in the industry claim (the tobacco makers) are going to go below the line and use demographics," Martin Bartle, public relations and communications director for Britain's Direct Marketing Association (DMA), told Reuters.

Below the line advertising refers to direct marketing, such as promotional mailings, coupons and tele-marketing. Traditional media advertising, including TV, radio, press and posters, is referred to as above the line.
Advertisers use the term through the line to describe campaigns that integrate media advertising with direct response efforts.

Next month the DMA will introduce a new code of practice that includes a series of regulations on tobacco marketing designed to ensure that tobacco products are promoted only to smokers over the legal age of 18.
DO BANS WORK?
While government and industry officials anticipate opposition from the tobacco companies, there is little accord on just how effective advertising bans are in curbing smoking.

"Advertising doesn't actually have any effect on the consumption at all," said the TMA's Carlisle. "We are aiming our advertising at our (existing) customers, not in any way to persuade people to take up smoking."
In Norway, where a ban on tobacco advertising was implemented in 1971, smoking among the young is now on the rise, Carlisle said.
"There are examples where bans haven't had an effect, but that's where they've been selective bans," countered the Health Education Authority spokesman.

A spokeswoman for the Department of Health said smoking in Norway among 13- to 15-year-olds fell by seven percent from 1975 to 1990. In France after a tobacco advertising ban was introduced in 1991, tobacco consumption dropped for the first time after 31 consecutive years of increases, she said.
But Carole Lehman, an associate with the London-based MVA Consultancy and author of a study on how school children are influenced by tobacco advertising, said the evidence is less clear.
"There has been evidence in France and Italy to show it wasn't a particularly marked effect," Lehman said. "It was affecting mainly brand choice, not smoking per se.
"It's quite a complex relationship and not a linear take-up between advertising and taking up smoking," she added.
HEALTH CHIEFS BATTLE HUGE AD SPEND
Britain already spends roughly 13 million pounds a year on smoking health education, including a five million pound anti-smoking campaign run by the the Health Education Authority.
The authority's spokesman, however, insisted that the government's efforts to educate the public about smoking is undermined by the tobacco industry's own advertising.

According to the TMA, the industry spends about 50 million pounds a year advertising tobacco in Britain, excluding about eight million pounds spent on sports sponsorship. The Health Education Authority thinks the figure is closer to 100 million.
The industry says it should not be permitted from advertising a legal product.
But the Health Education Authority spokesman said: "If cigarettes were being developed on the market now, they would be banned."
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
